582.title: Hanuman's first words
582.hook: honesty answered with honesty, and two princes carried up a mountain
582.howItsDone: Images of Hanuman carrying Rama and Lakshmana on his shoulders are common in Hindu art and temple sculpture, and devotees often speak of Hanuman as the one who carries others to Rama.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman's first words, and Rama praising a stranger's speech: not one word wrong, not too long, not rushed. Did you shape a sentence before you said it? Day five hundred eighty-two.

Now it's Lakshmana's turn to answer, and he does something you might not expect from a wary prince in a dangerous forest. He tells the stranger everything. Who they are. Why they're in exile. That Sita has been taken by a rakshasa while they were away, and they don't know where. That Kabandha sent them to find Sugriva. He holds nothing back. Most of us, meeting someone new, give the short version. Lakshmana gives the whole thing.
screen: `LAKSHMANA ANSWERS.` → `HE TELLS IT ALL.` → `NOT THE SHORT VERSION.`

segments.voice: First idea: trust answered with trust. Hanuman spoke carefully and honestly, and Lakshmana meets that honesty with his own. He even asks for help in so many words. Rama, he says, who used to be a refuge for others, has now come to Sugriva for refuge. That's a humbling sentence for a prince of Ayodhya to say out loud, and Lakshmana says it. Hanuman hears it and is glad. Your aim and Sugriva's are the same, he says. Sugriva too has lost his wife and his kingdom to someone stronger. You can help each other. Second idea: the disguise comes off. Hanuman drops the mendicant's form and takes his own shape: a monkey, the son of the Wind. And then he does something lovely and practical. Rishyamuka is steep, and the brothers have walked a long way. So he lifts them both onto his shoulders and carries them up the mountain to Sugriva. Third idea: the name. Hanuman is usually explained as the one with a notable jaw, from hanu, jaw. The story behind it, that as a baby he leapt at the rising sun thinking it was a fruit and was struck on the jaw by Indra's thunderbolt, is told later in the epic, when the monkeys need to remind him who he is. Today we see something simpler. A minister who listened well and spoke well, and then put two tired strangers on his shoulders and carried them uphill. Three days of first words, and they end not with a speech but with a lift.
screen: `TRUST ANSWERED WITH TRUST.` · `RAMA SEEKS REFUGE.` · `THE DISGUISE COMES OFF.` · `CARRIED UP THE MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Feel how much they carry on an ordinary day: bags, children, worries, other people's moods. Breathe in, and notice the weight. Breathe out, and let it slide off. Then, for a moment, picture someone you could help carry something this week: a chore, an errand, a heavy day. Just hold the thought, without planning. The bell holds the time.
Hanuman's first words. They end with the disguise dropped and two brothers carried up Rishyamuka on his shoulders.
Your line: Hanuman's first words. Today, answer someone's honesty with your own, and offer to carry one thing for them. Day five hundred eighty-two.

options: only your names.

583.title: the pact with Sugriva
583.hook: two exiles walk around a fire and become friends
583.howItsDone: In a Hindu wedding the couple walks around the sacred fire (often seven times, the saptapadi and pheras), and Agni is called on as witness; Rama and Sugriva's circling of the fire borrows that same gesture for friendship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman's first words ended with a lift, two brothers carried up the mountain on his shoulders. Did you carry something for someone? Day five hundred eighty-three.

Two exiles meet on a mountaintop. One is a prince who lost his kingdom and then his wife. The other is a monkey prince who lost his kingdom and then his wife. They've never seen each other before today. Both have been betrayed, or think they have. How do you start a friendship between two people with every reason to be careful? Valmiki's answer is very old, and it involves fire.
screen: `TWO EXILES MEET.` → `MATCHING LOSSES.` → `AN ANSWER WITH FIRE.`

segments.voice: Hanuman arranges it. He brings wood, kindles a fire between them, and honors it with flowers. Rama and Sugriva walk around the fire together, keeping it to their right, the way a bride and groom do at a Hindu wedding. Then they say to each other, in effect: from now on, your joy is my joy, and your sorrow is my sorrow. First idea: the witness. In Hindu ritual, Agni, the fire, carries offerings and witnesses vows. A friendship sworn in front of fire isn't a handshake. It's a promise made before a witness that can't be argued with. Second idea: they make it equal. Sugriva breaks off a flowering branch and spreads it on the ground, and he and Rama sit on it together. Hanuman breaks off another branch for Lakshmana. Two exiles, side by side on one branch. Neither is the patron and neither the beggar. Third idea: what each one needs. Sugriva tells Rama he's been robbed by his brother Vali, of his kingdom and his wife, and lives in fear on this mountain. Rama promises to kill Vali. Sugriva promises to help find Sita, wherever she is. It's a deal, yes. But the poem frames it as friendship first. The word for it is sakhya, the bond of a sakha, a friend. Centuries later, devotional teachers would count sakhya among the ways of loving God: as a friend. Here it starts plainly: two people with matching wounds, choosing each other.
screen: `AROUND THE FIRE, TOGETHER.` · `AGNI AS WITNESS.` · `TWO EXILES ON ONE BRANCH.` · `SAKHYA: FRIENDSHIP.`

segments.voice: Sit, and picture a small flame in front of you, a candle or a clay lamp. Bring to mind one friend. Breathe in, and remember a time their sorrow felt like yours. Breathe out, and remember a time their joy did too. Let that be your quiet promise for two minutes, no words required. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The pact with Sugriva. Sworn around a fire, your joy and sorrow mine, and sealed by sharing one branch.
Your line: the pact with Sugriva. Today, tell a friend you're on their side, plainly, out loud. Day five hundred eighty-three.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda 5 (the fire, the circling, the shared branch)
Bhagavata Purana 7.5.23 (sakhya among the forms of devotion)

584.title: the pact with Sugriva
584.hook: a bundle of jewels, and a brother-in-law who only knows the anklets
584.howItsDone: Touching the feet of parents, teachers and elders (pranam or charan sparsh) is a common gesture of respect in many Hindu families, and Lakshmana's words about the anklets are often quoted when it's explained.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the pact with Sugriva, sworn around a fire, two exiles on one branch. Did you tell a friend you're on their side? Day five hundred eighty-four.

Sugriva has something to show Rama. A while ago, he says, we were sitting up here, five of us, and we saw a rakshasa flying across the sky carrying a woman. She was crying out: Rama, Lakshmana. When she saw us below, she dropped her upper cloth and some of her jewelry, tied in a bundle. We kept them safe. He sends someone into the cave to bring them out.
screen: `FIVE OF US, ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `A WOMAN CRYING OUT.` → `A BUNDLE DROPPED.`

segments.voice: Rama sees the cloth and the ornaments and breaks down. He presses them to his chest and weeps. Sita did more than call to the forest. She left a trail. Passing over five strangers on a mountain, she threw down what she could, hoping someone would get it to Rama. And someone did. Then Rama turns to Lakshmana. Look, he says. Do you know these? And Lakshmana's answer is not what you'd expect. I don't know her armlets, he says. I don't know her earrings. But I know the anklets, because I bowed at her feet every day. Through all the years in the forest, Lakshmana kept his eyes lowered before his brother's wife. He looked at her feet, because that's where you look when you bow to someone you honor, an elder, a mother. So the anklets are what he knows. In many Indian families, touching an elder's feet is an everyday sign of respect, and this verse is often quoted to show what that respect can mean. Then the pact becomes real. Rama asks: who is he? Where did he take her? Sugriva admits he doesn't know where Ravana lives. But he promises he'll find out, and that Rama will have Sita back. Rama, still holding the jewelry, asks him to begin. A friendship sworn yesterday before the fire now has something to hold in its hands.
screen: `SITA LEFT A TRAIL.` · `I KNOW ONLY THE ANKLETS.` · `EYES LOWERED, IN RESPECT.` · `THE PACT HAS SOMETHING TO HOLD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your gaze drop to your own feet. Let it rest there, soft. Breathe in, and think of someone you honor: a parent, a teacher, an elder. Breathe out, and offer them, silently, the respect of a bow. No need to move. Let your eyes stay low and your breath slow, and keep that person in mind. The bell holds the time.
The pact with Sugriva. Today it holds Sita's dropped jewels, and Lakshmana recognizes only the anklets.
Your line: the pact with Sugriva. Today, show respect to one elder in a small, physical way: stand when they enter, greet them first, or listen fully. Day five hundred eighty-four.

585.title: the pact with Sugriva
585.hook: a feud built on a sealed cave, and one arrow through seven trees
585.howItsDone: The seven sala trees and Dundubhi's bones are favorite scenes in Ramayana art and storytelling, and sites near Hampi in Karnataka are traditionally linked to Kishkindha, Rishyamuka and Vali's cave.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the pact with Sugriva, and the anklets Lakshmana knew because he bowed at Sita's feet every day. Did you show an elder respect? Day five hundred eighty-five.

Rama has promised to kill Vali. Sugriva has a question he's too polite to ask out loud: can you? Vali is famous. He's so strong that he used to stride between the eastern and western seas before sunrise. Sugriva has watched that strength up close for years, and he has run from it across half the world. A friend with a bow is good news. But he needs to know this friend is enough. So Sugriva does two things. He tells a story. And then he points at some trees.
screen: `A QUESTION TOO POLITE TO ASK.` → `A STORY, THEN SOME TREES.`

segments.voice: First, the story of the brothers. Vali, the elder, ruled Kishkindha, and Sugriva served him and loved him. One night a demon named Mayavi came to the gate shouting a challenge. Vali chased him, with Sugriva following, into a huge cave. Wait at the mouth, Vali told his brother. A long time passed, about a year. Then blood came foaming out of the cave, and Sugriva heard the demon's roar but not his brother's voice. Sure Vali was dead, he sealed the cave with a boulder and went home, and the ministers made him king. But Vali wasn't dead. He'd killed the demon, came out, found the cave blocked and his brother on his throne, and believed he'd been betrayed. He drove Sugriva out and took his wife, Ruma. First idea: this feud grows out of a misunderstanding. Each brother, from where he stood, saw a betrayal. Second, the test. Sugriva shows Rama the dried skeleton of a buffalo demon named Dundubhi, which Vali once killed and flung a great distance. Rama flicks it away with his toe, far, far away. Sugriva, politely: it's dry now, it was much heavier then. So he points to seven huge sala trees. Vali could pierce one of these with an arrow, he says. Rama fires once. The arrow goes through all seven trees, through the hill behind them, into the earth, and returns to his quiver. Sugriva falls at his feet. Third: Sugriva's doubt is allowed. Nobody scolds him for asking for proof. The friendship survives an honest test.
screen: `MAYAVI AND THE SEALED CAVE.` · `EACH BROTHER SAW A BETRAYAL.` · `DUNDUBHI'S SKELETON.` · `ONE ARROW, SEVEN SALA TREES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone you're at odds with, or have drifted from. Breathe in, and ask: what did it look like from where they stood? You don't have to agree with them. Just picture the cave from the other side. Breathe out, and let your shoulders loosen. Stay with that one question, gently, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
The pact with Sugriva. Tested with a skeleton and seven sala trees, and one arrow goes through them all.
Your line: the pact with Sugriva. Today, if you doubt someone, ask them honestly, the way Sugriva did. Day five hundred eighty-five.

screen: `DAY 585 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: VALI'S DEATH AND TARA'S LAMENT.`

586.title: Vali's death and Tara's lament
586.hook: an arrow from cover, and a question the tradition still discusses
586.howItsDone: Vali's death is one of the most discussed episodes in Ramayana commentary and debate; traditional commentators defend Rama's action in several ways, while some later tellings and modern readers question it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the pact with Sugriva, tested: one arrow through seven sala trees. Did you ask an honest question instead of doubting quietly? Day five hundred eighty-six.

This is one of the hardest scenes in the Ramayana, and people have argued about it for centuries. Two brothers fight. A third person, hidden behind trees, shoots one of them. And the dying brother asks a question that every telling since has had to answer in its own way. You may have an opinion by the end. That's fine. The tradition has room for it. Today the job is simply to hear the scene as Valmiki tells it: who does what, who says what, and in what order.
screen: `ONE OF THE HARDEST SCENES.` → `AN ARROW FROM COVER.` → `THE DYING BROTHER'S QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Sugriva goes to Kishkindha's gate and roars a challenge. Vali comes out, and the brothers fight. Rama, watching from cover with his bow drawn, doesn't shoot. The brothers look so alike that he can't tell them apart. Sugriva is beaten and flees: why didn't you shoot? Rama explains, and Lakshmana hangs a flowering creeper around Sugriva's neck, so Rama will know him. Second challenge. This time Vali's wife Tara stops him at the door. She's wise, and she's worried. Sugriva lost an hour ago and he's back roaring, she says. He must have a powerful ally. I've heard it's Rama. Don't go. Vali goes anyway. Rama is righteous, he tells her; he won't do anything wrong. The fight begins, Vali starts to win, and Rama shoots. The arrow strikes Vali in the chest and he falls. Dying, Vali speaks to Rama, and it's an accusation. I wasn't fighting you. You struck from hiding while I fought someone else. What wrong had I done you? Rama answers him at length. This land is under the rule of Bharata's line, and I act for that rule. You took your brother's wife while he lived, a grave wrong. And kings hunt animals from cover. In the text, Vali accepts the answer and asks Rama's forgiveness. Many readers find Rama's answer sufficient. Others, for centuries, including commentators and poets, have found the scene troubling, and some later tellings change it. Valmiki lets both the question and the answer stand. Tomorrow, Tara.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS TOO ALIKE TO TELL.` · `TARA'S WARNING.` · `THE ARROW FROM COVER.` · `VALI'S QUESTION, RAMA'S ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Sit with a question that doesn't resolve easily. Maybe one from today's story, maybe one from your own life. Breathe in, and let it be there. Breathe out, and don't answer it. Just notice what it feels like to hold a hard question without forcing it shut. Come back to the breath each time you start arguing with yourself. The bell holds the time.
Vali's death and Tara's lament. Today, the arrow from cover, and Vali's question that the tradition still discusses.
screen: `VALI'S DEATH AND TARA'S LAMENT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Vali's death and Tara's lament. Today, when you disagree with someone, state the other side's best argument first. Day five hundred eighty-six.

587.title: Vali's death and Tara's lament
587.hook: a widow runs toward the battlefield, and the winner wishes he'd lost
587.howItsDone: Tara is honored in Hindu tradition as one of the panchakanya, five women named in a well-known verse recited in the morning; her lament for Vali is counted among the great laments of the epic.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vali's death and Tara's lament began, with an arrow from cover and the question he asked Rama. Did you state the other side's best argument? Day five hundred eighty-seven.

Word reaches the palace. The monkeys who saw it run back shouting: Vali is down. Most of them want to run, or hide, or shut the gates against Rama. Tara doesn't. She was the one who warned him, only hours ago, and he didn't listen. Now she runs the other way, out of the city, past the frightened crowd, toward the place where her husband is lying with an arrow in his chest. Her son Angada is with her.
screen: `VALI IS DOWN.` → `THE CROWD RUNS AWAY.` → `TARA RUNS TOWARD HIM.`

segments.voice: Tara reaches Vali and falls beside him. Her lament is long, and Valmiki gives it to her in full. She speaks to Vali: you lie on the bare earth as if you loved it more than me. She speaks to Sugriva, bitterly: now you have the kingdom. And she turns to Rama and asks him to kill her with the same arrow, so she can follow her husband. First idea: in the middle of an adventure story, the poem stops for a widow's grief, and lets it be angry. Tara isn't decoration. She warned Vali, and she was right. Second: Vali's last words. He speaks to Sugriva without anger now. Fate caught us both, he says, more or less. He asks him to care for Angada as his own son, and to listen to Tara, who understands things before anyone else does. He takes off the golden necklace that Indra once gave him and puts it on his brother. Then he dies. Third: Sugriva breaks. Now that he's won, he sees what winning cost. He says he would rather have his brother alive than the throne, and that he wants to die too. And Rama, the one who fired the arrow, is the one who has to steady them: he speaks to Tara, Sugriva and Angada about time, fate and duty, and tells them to perform the rites. Angada lights his father's pyre. A few days ago in the story, Rama gave a vulture a son's rites. Today a real son gives them to his father, and nobody in the scene is untouched.
screen: `TARA'S LAMENT, IN FULL.` · `VALI'S LAST WORDS TO SUGRIVA.` · `THE WINNER WISHES HE'D LOST.` · `ANGADA LIGHTS THE PYRE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind a loss, large or small, yours or someone else's. Don't push it away, and don't dive into it either. Breathe in, and let the feeling be exactly its real size. Breathe out, and let your body hold it. Tara's grief wasn't tidy, and yours doesn't need to be. Just sit with it, steadily, breath by breath. The bell holds the time.
Vali's death and Tara's lament. A widow's anger, a dying brother's necklace, and a winner who wishes he'd lost.

588.title: the rains
588.hook: a new king goes to his palace, and the man who made him king goes to a cave
588.howItsDone: The four months of the rainy season, chaturmasa, are still kept by many Hindu ascetics and households as a time to stay in one place, travel less, and take on extra vows and study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vali's death and Tara's lament. Angada lit his father's pyre, and Sugriva wished he'd lost. Did you listen without fixing? Today the week closes. Day five hundred eighty-eight.

Sugriva is crowned. Angada is named heir. The city celebrates with drums and garlands. And Rama doesn't go in. He's an exile, he says, and he promised fourteen years outside any village or town. So the new king of Kishkindha goes to his palace, and the man who made him king walks off to live in a cave. It's an odd picture, and Valmiki doesn't rush past it: the city lit up, and two brothers walking away from it into the hills.
screen: `SUGRIVA CROWNED.` → `RAMA WON'T GO IN.` → `TWO BROTHERS WALK TO THE HILLS.`

segments.voice: It's the start of the rainy season. Rama explains the plan: you can't send search parties across the land in the monsoon. Rivers flood, roads vanish. Enjoy your kingdom for these months, he tells Sugriva. When autumn comes, we search. So Rama and Lakshmana go to a mountain called Prasravana, the mountain of springs, and find a wide cave to wait out the rain. First idea: the hero waits. After the speed of the last weeks, the epic hits pause. Four months, and nothing to do but wait. For a man whose wife is a prisoner somewhere he can't even name, that may be the hardest stretch in the whole book. Action would be easier. Second: Lakshmana makes the waiting bearable. When Rama sinks into grief, Lakshmana reminds him who he is. Grief will wear you down, he says, more or less. Hold it until the time to act. Third: the place itself. Valmiki fills the cave chapter with what they see: peaks, rushing water, flowering trees, birds. The world goes on being lovely, even while you wait for the thing you need. Now the week, from the top. Lakshmana telling a stranger everything, and Hanuman carrying them up the mountain. A friendship sworn around a fire. Sita's anklets, known from bowing at her feet. Seven sala trees and one arrow. Vali's death, his question, and Tara's grief. And today, a crowning, a cave, and the rain coming in.
